statement: A three-digit number has three different digits, and its tens digit is the sum of its hundreds digit and its units digit. What is the largest such number?

choices.misconception: I found the smallest such number instead of the largest.
I made the units digit the sum of the other two digits instead of the tens digit.
I made the hundreds digit the sum of the other two digits instead of the tens digit.
I forgot that the three digits must all be different, and 9 + 0 = 9 repeats the 9.

hints: Make the hundreds digit as big as you can, then check.
Go greedy on the hundreds digit, but remember the tens digit is a sum, so it can be at most 9. Test each choice of hundreds digit against the rule that all digits differ.
With hundreds digit 9, the units digit must be 0 and the tens digit is then 9 again. Try hundreds digit 8.

solutions.reliable: The tens digit equals hundreds plus units, and it is at most 9. Hundreds digit 9 forces units digit 0 and tens digit 9, which repeats the 9, so it fails. Hundreds digit 8: units 0 gives tens 8, a repeat, while units 1 gives tens 9, and 891 has three different digits. No number starting with 8 can have a tens digit bigger than 9, so 891 is the largest. The transferable idea: to find the largest, fix the leading digit as high as the rules allow, then the next digit, checking every rule as you go.

whyOnTest: Digit puzzles reward a greedy search from the left, but only if every condition is checked, including that the digits differ.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
